case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a U.S. citizen has a constitutionally protected liberty interest that entitles her to due process—beyond a bare statutory citation—when a consular officer denies her noncitizen spouse’s immigrant visa, and what satisfies the ‘facially legitimate and bona fide reason’ standard for judicial review of that denial.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause); Immigration and Nationality Act inadmissibility provision cited in the denial, 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) (and, doctrinally, the consular nonreviewability/‘facially legitimate and bona fide’ framework governing visa denials).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Department of State argues that consular visa denials are largely insulated from judicial review (consular nonreviewability) and that, under the Supreme Court’s cases, the government satisfies any applicable standard by providing a facially valid statutory ground of inadmissibility (i.e., a statutory citation), without requiring courts to probe the underlying facts or demand more detailed explanations; the Ninth Circuit erred by effectively requiring additional factual disclosure or procedural process for a citizen-spouse and by expanding due-process constraints into the consular visa context.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Muñoz contends that denying her spouse’s immigrant visa burdens her own liberty interests as a U.S. citizen (including core family and marital interests) and therefore triggers due process protections; under Din as applied by the Ninth Circuit and related authority, the government must provide at least a facially legitimate and bona fide reason that is meaningfully reviewable—either by citing a statute with discrete factual predicates or by identifying facts that have a facial connection to the cited inadmissibility ground—so that the denial is not effectively unchallengeable and citizens are not forced to forfeit constitutional rights without process.
key_precedents: O’Bannon v. Town Court Nursing Center

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the most serious concern: that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is so open-textured a bare citation risks draining Mandel’s “facially legitimate and bona fide” inquiry of meaning. But under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din—as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh stress—the court’s role is not to demand a factual nexus to validate the Executive’s factfinding; it is to confirm a facially valid statutory ground and then stop absent a plausible, particularized allegation of bad faith. Justice Alito’s point about § 1182(b)(3) matters because Congress has affirmatively chosen to limit disclosure in security-related denials, and grafting a “minimal facts” requirement onto Mandel/Din would invite routine litigation, discovery pressure, and de facto merits review in a domain Trump v. Hawaii cautions is committed primarily to the political branches. I would therefore reverse on narrow grounds: statutory citation suffices here, leaving open only Din’s bad-faith exception and without deciding the full contours of any citizen-spouse liberty interest.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is purportedly too open-ended to be “bona fide” without some factual nexus, but that argument assumes the Fifth Amendment demands process in a domain the Constitution leaves principally to the political branches and where Congress has expressly limited disclosure, see 8 U.S.C. § 1182(b)(3). Even accepting arguendo a citizen-spouse interest, Mandel’s test is satisfied once the Executive invokes a valid statutory ground, and Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize) allows courts to look behind the reason only upon an affirmative showing of bad faith—not because a statute is broad. Trump v. Hawaii reinforces that courts do not second-guess individualized or security-related admissibility determinations beyond the facially legitimate inquiry, and respondents’ approach would effectively convert that narrow check into routine merits review. Under an originalist and separation-of-powers understanding of immigration admissions, the Ninth Circuit’s demand for more process is an unwarranted judicial expansion.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson argue that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is too open-ended to be “bona fide” without some factual nexus, but that proposed carveout has no footing in Mandel or Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din, which treated citation to a valid statutory ground as sufficient absent a plausible showing of bad faith. The statute’s breadth is a feature of Congress’s security-related scheme, and § 1182(b)(3) expressly reflects Congress’s judgment that further explanation may be withheld in precisely these cases—so demanding more factual disclosure effectively overrides that policy choice. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, expanding review to require additional factual exposition invites routine litigation and judicial second-guessing of sensitive law-enforcement and national-security determinations, contrary to the narrow role reaffirmed in Trump v. Hawaii. Because the Government provided a facially valid statutory basis and there is no adequate allegation of bad faith, the Ninth Circuit’s approach cannot be squared with Din/Mandel.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to stress Din’s administrability and the narrowness of Mandel review, and Justice Alito is correct that § 1182(b)(3) reflects Congress’s concern about disclosure in security cases. But Din’s controlling concurrence assumed the statutory ground itself meaningfully conveys that the Executive has made a fact-bound determination; where the Government invokes § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)—a capacious, security-adjacent label—a bare citation supplies no minimally intelligible factual nexus, risking that “facially legitimate and bona fide” becomes an empty formality for citizens asserting a serious family-integrity interest. I agree with Justice Jackson that requiring a high-level, non-sensitive factual connection does not invite merits second-guessing or discovery; it preserves Mandel’s limited check by ensuring the stated reason is not purely conclusory or pretextual. Congress’s choice to permit withholding details cannot erase the Fifth Amendment floor of minimally meaningful process in this narrow setting; it supports tailoring the remedy to a modest nexus rather than demanding sources, methods, or full evidentiary disclosure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best point that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is capacious, so a bare citation can feel like a label untethered to facts. But under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din, the administrable line is not “how determinate is the subsection,” it is whether the Government invoked a valid statutory ground and whether the plaintiff has made a plausible, particularized showing of bad faith; adding a “minimal factual nexus” requirement would inevitably pull courts into evaluating the adequacy of explanations in security cases, the very merits-probing Mandel and Trump v. Hawaii resist. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito persuasively connect that administrability concern to Congress’s disclosure choices in § 1182(b)(3), which would be in tension with a judicially imposed obligation to provide additional factual exposition. I would therefore reverse while emphasizing Din’s narrow bad-faith pathway as the appropriate safeguard against pretext.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the case’s hardest point: § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is broad enough that a bare citation can feel like an empty label, risking a hollow “bona fide” inquiry. But under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress—the court’s role is limited to confirming a facially valid statutory basis and stopping absent a plausible, particularized allegation of bad faith; nothing in that rule turns on how “determinate” the subsection’s predicates are. Requiring a “minimal factual nexus” is not a modest tweak but a doctrinal expansion that would predictably force merits-adjacent probing (and pressures for disclosure) in the very security context where Congress signaled constrained explanations in § 1182(b)(3). Trump v. Hawaii reinforces that the judiciary should not repackage substantive review as procedural sufficiency in admissions decisions entrusted to the political branches.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best point that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is open-textured, so a bare citation can look like a conclusory label rather than a fact-linked reason. But under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize—the doctrinal line is administrable and historically grounded: a facially valid INA citation is “facially legitimate,” and it is “bona fide” absent a plausible, particularized allegation of bad faith; the statute’s breadth does not itself supply the needed allegation. Adding a “minimal factual nexus” requirement would, in practice, invite routine litigation over the sufficiency of consular explanations and pressure disclosure in the very security-adjacent context where Congress in § 1182(b)(3) contemplated limited explanation, effectively expanding judicial supervision beyond Mandel/Din and what Trump v. Hawaii reaffirmed. I therefore remain with petitioner: the inquiry ends with the statutory ground here because respondents have not made the kind of affirmative bad-faith showing Din requires.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s best point is that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is open-textured, so a bare citation may seem too conclusory to be “bona fide.” But under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din—correctly emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan—the inquiry does not turn on how “discrete” the subsection’s factual predicates are; it turns on whether the Government invoked a valid statutory ground and whether the plaintiff makes a plausible, affirmative showing of bad faith. Textually, § 1182(b)(3) reflects Congress’s judgment that, in security-related contexts, the Government may withhold further explanation, and importing a “minimal factual nexus” requirement would risk reintroducing merits review and disclosure pressures through the back door in tension with Mandel as reaffirmed in Trump v. Hawaii. Absent a particularized bad-faith allegation, I do not see a doctrinally anchored basis to require more than the statutory citation here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively stress Din’s administrability: a valid statutory citation usually ends the inquiry absent a plausible bad-faith allegation, and § 1182(b)(3) reflects Congress’s sensitivity to disclosure in security-related denials. But that argument assumes the cited subsection itself provides a meaningful “reason” capable of being assessed for facial bona fides; with § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)’s unusually open-textured “may engage” standard, a bare citation risks functioning as a conclusory label rather than a fact-linked rationale, making even Din’s limited good-faith check largely illusory. Justice Alito’s separation-of-powers point is important, yet requiring a minimally non-sensitive factual nexus (e.g., the general type of conduct or association at issue) does not invite merits probing or discovery; it is a modest procedural floor that preserves Mandel’s promise of a facially bona fide reason without undermining § 1182(b)(3) or Trump v. Hawaii’s caution against second-guessing. Because the Government can satisfy this requirement without revealing sources and methods, I do not think the petitioners’ rule sufficiently safeguards procedural fairness where a citizen-spouse’s interest is implicated.

John Roberts.reasoning: Assuming arguendo that a citizen-spouse has some protected liberty interest, our precedent in Kleindienst v. Mandel and the controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din (Kennedy, J.) require only that the Government provide a "facially legitimate and bona fide reason" for the visa denial, and absent an affirmative showing of bad faith courts may not look behind that determination. A consular officer’s citation to a valid inadmissibility ground in the INA—here 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)—is facially legitimate, and, under Din, ordinarily suffices as bona fide without forcing disclosure of sensitive facts or inviting broader judicial inquiry that would undermine the political branches’ primacy in immigration. The Ninth Circuit’s demand for additional factual exposition effectively expands due process into an area long governed by limited review and consular nonreviewability, risking institutional legitimacy by prompting courts to supervise individualized visa decisions. A narrow disposition adhering to Din and Mandel respects precedent and federalism by leaving visa-admissibility judgments to the Executive subject only to the limited bad-faith exception.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution’s text does not confer on a U.S. citizen a freestanding Fifth Amendment liberty entitlement to have a noncitizen spouse admitted, and admission of aliens is committed in the first instance to the political branches under Congress’s plenary power. Even assuming arguendo some protected interest, Mandel’s limited review governs, and once the Executive provides a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” courts may not “look behind” the denial. Under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din, a consular officer satisfies that standard by citing a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility such as 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii), without requiring further factual disclosure or judicial probing. The Ninth Circuit’s demand for more process improperly expands due process into the consular-visa context and conflicts with Mandel/Din’s narrow, deferential framework.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Even assuming arguendo that a citizen-spouse can assert a cognizable liberty interest, Mandel limits judicial review to whether the Government offered a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” and Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din (which I joined) holds that a consular officer satisfies that standard by citing a relevant statutory ground of inadmissibility without judicial probing of underlying facts. Here, the consular officer’s citation to 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is facially valid and thus ends the inquiry under Mandel/Din, particularly given Congress’s judgment that security-related inadmissibility determinations need not be accompanied by further explanation, see 8 U.S.C. § 1182(b)(3). The Ninth Circuit’s demand for additional factual disclosure effectively expands due process and invites intrusive review of sensitive national-security and law-enforcement judgments, contrary to the narrow scope reaffirmed in Trump v. Hawaii and the longstanding doctrine of consular nonreviewability. Accordingly, the judgment below should be reversed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A U.S. citizen’s marital and family integrity interests are weighty liberty interests protected by the Fifth Amendment, and government action that effectively forecloses reunification through an immigrant visa denial warrants at least minimally meaningful process rather than an unreviewable conclusory citation. While Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din applied Mandel to accept a statutory citation to § 1182(a)(3)(B), it did so in a context where the citation itself signaled a bona fide factual determination; where, as here, the government relies on § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii), which lacks discrete factual predicates, due process and Mandel’s “facially legitimate and bona fide reason” standard are not satisfied by a bare statutory label untethered to any facially connected facts. Consistent with Trump v. Hawaii’s reaffirmation of Mandel’s limited review, courts need not probe the merits or classified evidence, but the citizen-spouse is entitled to enough factual disclosure to permit a non-frivolous determination that the stated ground is facially legitimate and not pretextual. Requiring that minimal factual nexus protects access to justice for citizens and prevents the consular nonreviewability doctrine from swallowing constitutional guarantees.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Assuming arguendo the citizen-spouse has a protected liberty interest, our controlling framework under Mandel requires only a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” and Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din (under Marks) indicates that a consular officer satisfies that standard by citing a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility without further factual exposition. A citation to 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is facially legitimate because it is an express INA basis for inadmissibility, and it is bona fide absent a plausible showing of bad faith, which Din treats as the narrow opening for further inquiry. Requiring additional factual disclosure would undermine the workability and administrability of consular nonreviewability and expand due-process constraints into an area where Congress and the Executive have primary responsibility, consistent with the limited review reaffirmed in Trump v. Hawaii. Because the Ninth Circuit effectively demanded more than Din permits, I would reverse.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Constitution assigns Congress plenary authority over the admission of aliens, and the judiciary’s role in reviewing consular visa denials is correspondingly narrow under the longstanding “facially legitimate and bona fide reason” framework of Kleindienst v. Mandel. Under Marks, the controlling opinion in Kerry v. Din is Justice Kennedy’s concurrence, which held that even assuming arguendo a citizen-spouse has a protected liberty interest, the government satisfies due process by citing a valid INA inadmissibility provision—there, 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(B)—without further factual disclosure absent an affirmative showing of bad faith. Requiring more than a statutory citation (here, § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)) would invite courts to second-guess sensitive executive judgments in an area where Congress has delegated decisionmaking to the political branches, contrary to separation-of-powers principles reflected again in Trump v. Hawaii. Because the Ninth Circuit effectively demanded additional explanation beyond Din’s rule, I would reverse and hold the statutory citation suffices unless the plaintiff plausibly alleges bad faith.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Kleindienst v. Mandel, when the Executive denies a visa on the basis of a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” courts may not “look behind” that decision or reweigh it against the citizen’s asserted interests. Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din applied Mandel and concluded that the government satisfied that standard by citing a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility with discrete predicates, without requiring additional factual disclosure or probing of the underlying evidence; that approach preserves the traditional, workable limits of consular nonreviewability. Here, the consular officer’s citation to 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) provides a facially legitimate reason tied to Congress’s inadmissibility scheme, and absent a plausible allegation of bad faith, due process does not require more process or a fuller explanation. Expanding judicial review to demand factual elaboration would depart from history and tradition in immigration admissions and risk substantial practical and institutional consequences by inviting routine merits litigation over consular determinations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Assuming arguendo that a citizen-spouse possesses some protected liberty interest, our precedents constrain judicial review of consular visa denials to the Mandel inquiry, which asks only whether the Government has provided a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason.” Under Marks, Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din holds that a consular officer’s citation to a valid INA inadmissibility provision—there, 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(B), and here § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)—suffices and does not require additional factual disclosure or judicial probing of the underlying evidence. That approach is methodologically consistent with Kleindienst v. Mandel and reaffirmed in Trump v. Hawaii, which cautions against expanding due-process or merits review into an area textually committed to the political branches. The Ninth Circuit therefore erred to the extent it required more than a facial statutory basis to satisfy due process in this context.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The denial of a citizen’s spouse’s immigrant visa implicates a significant liberty interest in family integrity, and at minimum triggers the limited procedural protection recognized in Mandel’s “facially legitimate and bona fide reason” framework as applied through Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din. A bare citation to 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)—a provision lacking discrete factual predicates—does not meaningfully satisfy that standard because it provides no fact-based basis to assess whether the government actually relied on a bona fide reason, consistent with the Ninth Circuit’s approach in Cardenas. Requiring a minimal factual link (without authorizing probing merits review) respects consular nonreviewability while providing basic procedural fairness under the Fifth Amendment and aligns with Trump v. Hawaii’s understanding that courts may ensure the government has offered a facially valid, good-faith justification. Accordingly, due process here requires more than an opaque statutory label when the statute itself does not cabin the factual grounds for denial.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a U.S. citizen has a constitutional due process right to a more particularized explanation (and limited judicial review) when a consular officer denies a noncitizen spouse’s immigrant visa, or whether citing a statutory ground of inadmissibility alone satisfies the governing standard and ends the inquiry under consular nonreviewability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause); 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) (inadmissibility for seeking to enter to engage in unlawful activity) as an example of the cited inadmissibility provision; doctrine of consular nonreviewability (judge-made).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Department of State and other federal petitioners argue that longstanding consular nonreviewability bars courts from second-guessing visa denials and that, under the controlling ‘facially legitimate and bona fide reason’ standard (as discussed in Kerry v. Din and referenced in Trump v. Hawaii), the government satisfies any obligation by identifying a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility; they contend the Ninth Circuit improperly expanded due process and judicial review by requiring more factual disclosure or a tighter factual match, risking disruption to immigration and national-security-related visa adjudications.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Muñoz and the other respondents argue that a U.S. citizen has a protected liberty interest implicated by the denial of a spouse’s visa (or at least an interest sufficient to trigger minimal due process), and that a bare statutory citation—especially to a broadly worded ground like § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) lacking ‘discrete factual predicates’—does not satisfy Din’s requirement unless the statute itself is fact-specific or the record contains facts that supply a facial connection to the cited ground; they also argue it is impermissible to force a citizen to choose between living in the United States and maintaining marital life without due process, and that unlike situations where other parties can effectively vindicate the affected interests, no one else can realistically raise these due process concerns if courts refuse review.
key_precedents: O’Bannon v. Town Court Nursing Center, 447 U.S. 773 (1980)
Cardenas v. United States (Ninth Circuit decision summarizing Din, as referenced in the materials)
D.C. Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983) (referenced for certiorari/percolation discussion in the provided excerpt, not as a merits precedent on visas)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best objection: that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is so capacious that a bare citation risks becoming an unreviewable label, leaving the “facially legitimate and bona fide” inquiry empty. But under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din, the constitutional check is not calibrated to the breadth of Congress’s drafting; it is a narrow inquiry satisfied when the Government invokes a valid statutory ground, subject only to a plausible bad-faith exception. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Congress’s decision in § 1182(b)(3) to restrict explanations in security-adjacent denials reinforces—rather than undermines—that courts should not constitutionalize a “factual tether” requirement that would invite looking behind consular decisions and discovery, which Trump v. Hawaii cautions against. A narrow reversal that assumes without deciding any liberty interest and holds that the statutory citation suffices absent a plausible allegation of bad faith best adheres to precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is broad and therefore a bare citation provides little notice, but that objection asks us to constitutionalize a disclosure obligation the Fifth Amendment’s text does not impose and that Congress has not required—indeed, Congress has limited explanations for security-related denials in § 1182(b)(3). Under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the Executive satisfies Mandel once it identifies a valid statutory ground, and courts may not demand a tighter factual match or additional facts absent a plausible showing of bad faith. Trump v. Hawaii reinforces that the judiciary’s role here is exceptionally limited in light of the political Branches’ primary authority over admission of aliens and the longstanding doctrine of consular nonreviewability. Because respondents offer no plausible bad-faith allegation, the Ninth Circuit’s more searching approach improperly displaces the political Branches and lacks any foundation in the Constitution’s original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is so capacious that a bare statutory citation risks becoming an unreviewable label and invites arbitrariness. But that proposed cure—a judicially enforced “factual tether” requirement keyed to statutory breadth—would necessarily require courts to look behind the consular officer’s stated basis and to constitutionalize a disclosure obligation that Congress has not imposed and in related contexts has curtailed (as Justice Gorsuch notes regarding § 1182(b)(3)). Under Mandel as applied through Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din, the Executive satisfies the “facially legitimate and bona fide” standard by identifying a valid statutory ground absent a plausible allegation of bad faith; Trump v. Hawaii underscores the administrability and separation-of-powers costs of expanding that threshold inquiry into fact-matching litigation. I therefore remain with the Chief Justice’s view that the Ninth Circuit’s approach is inconsistent with Din’s limited bad-faith backstop and would erode consular nonreviewability in security-adjacent adjudications.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability argument—statutory citation plus a bad-faith safety valve—has force, especially in light of Trump v. Hawaii’s separation-of-powers caution, but it assumes the citation itself conveys a meaningfully reviewable “reason.” Here, as Justice Jackson underscores, § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)’s capacious “unlawful activity” label lacks the kind of discrete factual predicates Justice Kennedy relied on in Din; accepting a bare citation would convert “facially legitimate and bona fide” into a purely formal incantation and leave citizen spouses with no minimal protection against arbitrariness. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 1182(b)(3) cuts toward deference, but it is best read as a targeted nondisclosure rule for specified security-related grounds—not a constitutional license to provide no nonclassified, particularized factual tether when the Government chooses an unusually broad inadmissibility provision. A narrow requirement of some facial factual connection (without merits probing or discovery) preserves consular nonreviewability while keeping Mandel/Din’s threshold inquiry from collapsing into unreviewable labeling.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is so capacious a bare citation risks becoming an empty label—has force as a notice-and-arbitrariness concern, but under Mandel as applied in Justice Kennedy’s controlling Din concurrence the constitutional inquiry is deliberately modest: once the Government invokes a valid statutory ground, courts do not ratchet up required factual disclosure based on statutory breadth absent a plausible bad-faith showing. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on § 1182(b)(3) matters for my textualist instincts: Congress affirmatively calibrated the level of explanation in security-adjacent denials, and a judicially imposed “factual tether” rule would conflict with that statutory structure and invite courts to look behind consular decisions in a way Mandel forbids. Justice Jackson’s proposed “facial factual connection” standard is attractive in the abstract, but in application it risks devolving into case-by-case policing of how much linkage is enough, undermining administrability and recreating merits review through the back door. I would therefore reverse, while preserving Din’s narrow bad-faith safety valve for genuinely non-bona-fide invocations.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s core concern—that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is so broad a citation becomes an empty label—has force as a policy critique, but it does not fit our controlling doctrinal and separation-of-powers limits. As the Chief and Justice Kagan note, Din (Kennedy, J., concurring) treats the Mandel inquiry as satisfied when the Executive invokes a valid statutory ground, with further judicial probing only upon a plausible showing of bad faith; recalibrating that rule based on statutory breadth would require courts to "look behind" consular decisions and invite precisely the discovery and merits review Mandel forbids. Congress’s choice in § 1182(b)(3) to restrict explanations in security-adjacent denials reinforces that courts should not constitutionalize an extra-statutory disclosure obligation, and Trump v. Hawaii underscores the workability and institutional necessity of that limited check. Absent a plausible bad-faith allegation here, I do not see a legal basis to impose a “facial factual connection” requirement that would effectively rewrite Din.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is broad and can feel like “no reason at all” is the best argument for respondents, but it effectively asks us to recalibrate Mandel/Din based on how Congress drafts inadmissibility categories. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Din makes the constitutional inquiry turn on whether the Government has invoked a valid statutory ground and whether the plaintiff plausibly alleges bad faith; it does not create a sliding-scale “factual tether” requirement keyed to statutory breadth. Congress’s decision in § 1182(b)(3) to limit explanations in security-related denials reinforces that courts should not constitutionalize additional disclosure that would, in practice, invite “looking behind” consular decisions—precisely what Trump v. Hawaii warns against for administrability and separation-of-powers reasons. Absent a plausible bad-faith allegation, the statutory citation suffices and the Ninth Circuit’s “factual match” approach is inconsistent with our precedents and institutional limits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s concern that § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is too capacious to be “facially legitimate and bona fide” without a factual tether is the best argument for affirmance, but it asks us to revise the Mandel/Din framework by making constitutional adequacy turn on statutory breadth rather than on the presence of a valid statutory ground plus a bad-faith safety valve. Under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din, the “facial” inquiry is satisfied when the Government cites a statutory basis for inadmissibility, and further probing is permitted only upon an affirmative showing of bad faith; the Ninth Circuit’s demand for more particularized facts effectively invites courts to “look behind” the reason in the ordinary case. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, Congress’s choice in § 1182(b)(3) to limit disclosure in security-related denials confirms that courts should be reluctant to constitutionalize an additional narrative requirement that Congress withheld. Trump v. Hawaii reinforces that administrable deference is especially warranted in this domain, and the proposed “factual match” threshold risks converting a limited facial check into merits review and discovery over consular determinations.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively stress administrability and § 1182(b)(3)’s limits on disclosure, and I agree Mandel/Din and Trump v. Hawaii forbid courts from probing the merits of consular decisions or ordering discovery absent bad faith. But that deference presupposes that the Government has actually supplied a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” and with § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)’s exceptionally capacious “unlawful activity” label, a bare citation risks making the threshold inquiry purely formal—functionally insulating arbitrary decisionmaking while deeply impacting a citizen spouse’s interests. Justice Gorsuch’s concern that any “factual connection” test invites looking behind the decision is real, yet a minimal nonclassified factual tether (without evaluating accuracy or sufficiency) is a procedural-fairness check consistent with Din’s premise that the reason be meaningfully connected to the statutory ground. Trump v. Hawaii reinforces deference after the threshold is met; it does not require us to treat an undefined label as automatically meeting that threshold in every case.

John Roberts.reasoning: Consular nonreviewability remains a foundational, long-settled limitation on judicial intrusion into visa decisions, and our cases indicate that when the Executive cites a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility, courts generally do not look behind it. Under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din, 576 U.S. 86 (2015), the government satisfies the “facially legitimate and bona fide reason” requirement by identifying the statutory basis for denial, absent a plausible showing of bad faith; Trump v. Hawaii, 138 S. Ct. 2392 (2018), reaffirmed that deferential approach in the immigration context. Requiring a more particularized factual explanation and permitting discovery to test the evidentiary basis would expand due process in a way that risks undermining institutional legitimacy and embroiling courts in sensitive immigration and national-security judgments tied to 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii). A narrow ruling reversing the Ninth Circuit and applying Din’s bad-faith-limited framework preserves precedent while leaving political-branch avenues for additional disclosure where appropriate.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution assigns the political Branches primary authority over the admission of aliens, and the Due Process Clause does not confer on a U.S. citizen a judicially enforceable right to compel a consular officer to provide a more particularized explanation for denying a noncitizen spouse’s visa beyond what Congress has required. Under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din, when the Executive identifies a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility—such as 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)—that citation supplies a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason” and ends the inquiry absent a plausible showing of bad faith. Expanding review to demand additional factual disclosure or a tighter factual match would improperly displace the political Branches’ immigration judgments and contradict the limited form of review reiterated in Trump v. Hawaii. The Ninth Circuit’s approach effectively creates a new due-process entitlement untethered to the Constitution’s text and original public meaning and inconsistent with the longstanding doctrine of consular nonreviewability.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Kleindienst v. Mandel, when the Executive excludes an alien on the basis of a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” courts do not look behind that determination, and that limited inquiry applies even when a U.S. citizen asserts an interest affected by the denial. Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din indicates the government satisfies Mandel by identifying a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility, absent a plausible showing of bad faith; requiring additional factual disclosure or a tighter “factual match” invites precisely the probing review Mandel forbids. Here, citation to 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is a facially legitimate basis for inadmissibility, and practical consequences for immigration and national-security adjudications counsel strongly against expanding due-process-driven judicial oversight of consular decisions. Trump v. Hawaii confirms the Court’s continued reliance on Mandel’s deferential framework in sensitive immigration contexts, reinforcing that the Ninth Circuit’s approach improperly erodes consular nonreviewability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A U.S. citizen’s marital relationship and ability to live with a spouse in this country implicate a substantial liberty interest under the Fifth Amendment, and due process is not satisfied by a bare statutory citation that provides no meaningful notice or check against arbitrariness. Under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din, the government may rely on a statutory ground alone when that provision supplies “discrete factual predicates,” but 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) is so open-ended (“unlawful activity”) that it risks effectively unreviewable discretion without at least some minimal, facially connecting factual explanation. Consular nonreviewability cannot be treated as an absolute bar where the government’s stated reason is too indefinite to be “facially legitimate and bona fide” in any practical sense, especially given the severe real-world impact on citizens and families. Limited judicial review requiring a particularized, nonclassified explanation (or a facial factual connection in the record) appropriately balances deference in immigration with basic fairness and access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Even assuming the citizen spouse has some cognizable due process interest, the governing inquiry under Mandel is limited to whether the Government has provided a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” and courts may not “look behind” that reason once given. Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din treated the Government’s citation of a valid inadmissibility provision as sufficient to satisfy that standard, absent a showing of bad faith, and Trump v. Hawaii reaffirmed the narrowness and workability of that approach in the immigration context. Requiring consular officers to provide a more particularized factual account for broadly worded grounds like 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) would expand judicial review in tension with consular nonreviewability and Congress’s allocation of responsibility over admissions. A rule that treats a statutory citation as adequate (subject to a plausible bad-faith exception) best preserves statutory coherence and administrable limits while respecting the separation-of-powers concerns underlying the doctrine.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Mandel’s “facially legitimate and bona fide reason” framework, once the Executive identifies a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility, courts may not “look behind” that determination absent a plausible showing of bad faith. Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din applied that rule and treated the government’s citation of a congressionally enacted inadmissibility provision as sufficient, which forecloses the Ninth Circuit’s demand for additional factual disclosure or a tighter factual match. Requiring more would also trench on separation-of-powers principles in immigration and override Congress’s choice in 8 U.S.C. § 1182(b)(3) to limit explanations for security-related denials. Whatever due process interests a citizen spouse may have, the modest Mandel/Din inquiry is satisfied here by the statutory citation, and consular nonreviewability bars further judicial reexamination.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the judge-made doctrine of consular nonreviewability, courts generally may not second-guess a consular officer’s visa denial, and the narrow constitutional safety valve is the “facially legitimate and bona fide reason” test from Kleindienst v. Mandel as applied in Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din. Din indicates that, absent a plausible allegation of bad faith, the government satisfies that standard by identifying a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility, and courts may not “look behind” that reason to demand additional factual detail. Requiring a more particularized explanation for denials under provisions like 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) would expand due process and judicial review into an area where Congress and the Executive have primary responsibility and where practical workability and national-security sensitivities counsel restraint. Trump v. Hawaii confirms the Court’s reluctance to probe executive immigration determinations beyond that limited Mandel/Din framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Assuming without deciding that a U.S. citizen’s interests are implicated by a spouse’s visa denial, the governing standard under Kleindienst v. Mandel as applied in Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din requires only a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” after which courts may not “look behind” the decision absent an affirmative showing of bad faith. A consular officer’s citation to a valid statutory ground of inadmissibility—such as 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii)—is facially legitimate, and nothing in the Due Process Clause’s text or our precedents supports a constitutional requirement that the Executive provide further factual disclosure or that courts conduct a tighter factual match. Trump v. Hawaii confirms the Court’s adherence to Mandel/Din in this domain, reflecting the longstanding principle of consular nonreviewability and the institutional limits on judicial review of visa determinations intertwined with foreign affairs and national security. The Ninth Circuit’s demand for more particularized explanation effectively expands judicial review beyond what Din permits and is inconsistent with methodological constraints imposed by precedent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Due Process Clause protects U.S. citizens from arbitrary governmental deprivations when the Government’s action effectively forces a choice between residing in the United States and maintaining a marital life, so at least minimal process is required when a spouse’s immigrant visa is denied. Under Justice Kennedy’s controlling concurrence in Kerry v. Din, the Government must provide a “facially legitimate and bona fide reason,” which is not invariably satisfied by a bare citation to an overbroad inadmissibility provision like 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(A)(ii) that lacks discrete factual predicates; absent some fact in the record that supplies a facial connection, the explanation risks being functionally unreviewable and thus inconsistent with procedural fairness. Trump v. Hawaii confirms courts do not second-guess the merits once a facially legitimate and bona fide reason is supplied, but it does not eliminate the threshold requirement of a reason that is meaningfully tethered to the statutory ground. Limited judicial review to ensure that threshold is met (and to police bad faith under Din) respects consular nonreviewability while preventing arbitrary deprivations of a citizen’s protected interests.
